title: Chronic Serotonergic Overstimulation Mimicking Panic Attacks in a Patient with Parkinson's Disease Receiving Additional Antidepressant Treatment with Moclobemide
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of idiopathic Parkinson’s disease presented with 4 months of recurrent, unpredictable episodes of jitteriness, perioral and acral formications, palpitations, thoracic tightness, transient hypertension, and a dark red flush of the scalp and neck. She denied fever or altered sensorium. Three months earlier she had been evaluated in an emergency department for chest pain and dyspnea; ECG, echocardiography, and blood work were normal, and she was diagnosed with arterial hypertension and started on ranolazine. Symptoms recurred despite ranolazine; a β-blocker was initiated but discontinued by the patient due to lack of benefit. She had no history of asthma or acute respiratory illness. Her medical history was notable for obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP and chronic hypothyroidism on levothyroxine.  
Her medications at admission were moclobemide 450 mg/day, agomelatine 50 mg/day, pramipexole 0.525 mg/day, rasagiline 1 mg/day, levodopa/benserazide retard 200/50 mg/day, ranolazine 375 mg/day, and levothyroxine 100 μg/day. The moclobemide dose had been raised from 150 mg to 450 mg about 1 year earlier.  
On examination she was alert, oriented, and calm. Neurologic exam showed moderate right upper-extremity rigidity and adiadochokinesia; gait was normal with no tremor. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There was severe insomnia and daytime fatigue; mood was intermittently depressed. Vital signs: BP 140/80 mmHg, HR 84 beats/min, T 36.4°C.  
Differential diagnoses considered at admission for the paroxysmal psychovegetative episodes included panic disorder, somatoform autonomic disorder, arterial hypertension with hypertensive exacerbations, iatrogenic hyperthyroidism, asthmatic disorder, and drug-induced serotonin toxicity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Panic disorder was considered because of abrupt anxiety and autonomic symptoms — “with a working diagnosis of panic disorder.” It was less likely when “no further episodic psychovegetative or panic-related symptoms occurred during hospitalization.”  
2. Somatoform autonomic disorder was considered given the unexplained autonomic disturbances — “Differential diagnoses … included … somatoform autonomic disorder.” It was deemed unlikely after symptom resolution following medication changes.  
3. Arterial hypertension with hypertensive exacerbations was considered due to transient elevations in blood pressure — “Differential diagnoses … included … arterial hypertension with hypertensive exacerbations.” It was ruled out when “the discontinuation of ranolazine … did not result in changes of blood pressure, we could also rule out arterial hypertension as a causative factor.”  
4. Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism was considered because of her thyroid replacement therapy — “Differential diagnoses … included … iatrogenic hyperthyroidism.” It was excluded when “blood work showed normal thyroid parameters, and no remarkable structural abnormalities of the thyroid gland were detected by sonography. Thus, we could rule out the possibility of iatrogenic hyperthyroidism.”  
5. Asthmatic disorder was considered due to episodes of dyspnea and chest tightness — “Differential diagnoses … included … asthmatic disorder.” It became unlikely in the absence of respiratory findings and because symptoms resolved independently of asthma therapy.  
6. Drug-induced serotonin toxicity was considered given her treatment with MAO-A and MAO-B inhibitors — “Differential diagnoses … included … drug-induced serotonin toxicity.” It was supported when “moclobemide, rasagiline, and ranolazine were discontinued” and the patient “experienced a decrease of psychovegetative symptoms.”
